paper_name: Fast Imitation via Behavior Foundation Models

basic_idea: Leverage behavior foundation models (BFMs) based on successor measures to achieve imitation learning with few expert demonstrations.
BFMs can imitate expert behavior almost instantly with just a few demonstrations, without requiring reinforcement learning (RL) or fine-tuning.

The proposed FB-IL (Forward-Backward Imitation Learning) methods are compatible with various imitation learning principles including behavioral cloning, feature matching, and reward-based and goal-based reductions.
motivation: Existing imitation learning (IL) approaches often require numerous demonstrations for new tasks.
Current IL methods frequently necessitate extensive interaction with the environment or running complex reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms for each new imitation task.
Some IL methods require prior knowledge of the family of behaviors to be imitated.
The computation needed to derive an imitation policy for a new behavior is often high, leading to long processing times.
research_question: Can behavior foundation models based on successor measures accurately solve imitation learning tasks from few demonstrations without additional samples or solving complex reinforcement learning problems?
Can a behavior foundation model accurately solve imitation tasks with minimal inference time?
Is a behavior foundation model compatible with different imitation learning formalizations such as behavioral cloning, apprenticeship learning, and reward-based or goal-based reductions?
How does the performance of imitation learning via RL foundation models compare to state-of-the-art offline imitation learning algorithms when using a single expert demonstration?
How does the time required to produce an imitation policy from new demonstrations using RL foundation models compare to traditional offline imitation learning methods?
method: Pre-train a behavior foundation model (BFM) using unsupervised transitions/trajectories without prior knowledge of specific behaviors to be imitated.
Utilize the Forward-Backward (FB) framework, which learns a tractable representation of successor measures, to build BFMs.
The FB framework learns two maps, F (forward) and B (backward), and a set of parametrized policies (pi_z).
The FB model approximates successor measures M_pi(s0, a0, X) using the learned F and B maps: M_pi(s0, a0, X) approx integral_X F(s0, a0, z)^T B(s) rho(ds).
The learned policies are defined as pi_z(s) approx argmax_a F(s, a, z)^T z.
Implement Behavioral Cloning (BC) by minimizing the negative log-likelihood of expert actions under the FB-learned policies pi_z, optimizing over z: L_BC(z) = -E_tau sum_t ln(pi_z(a_t|s_t)).
Implement reward-based imitation learning by setting the z parameter based on inferred reward functions.
For empirical reward (ER_FB), set z = E_s~rho [r(s)B(s)], where r(s) is proportional to the expert state distribution rho_e(s) divided by the unsupervised dataset state distribution rho(s).
For regularized empirical reward (RER_FB), set z based on a formula involving the covariance of B and expectations over expert states.
Implement feature matching (FM_FB) by minimizing the squared difference between the B-features of states visited under the imitation policy and the expert policy.
Implement distribution matching (DM_FB) by minimizing the L2 norm difference between the successor measures of the imitation policy and the expert policy.
Implement Bellman residual minimization for distribution matching (BBELLFB) by minimizing the Bellman gaps of Q-functions for rewards linearly spanned by B.
Implement goal-based imitation learning (GOALFB) by setting a time-varying z parameter corresponding to a future state in the expert trajectory as the goal.
For FB-IL methods requiring gradient descent over z (e.g., BC_FB, BBELLFB, FM_FB), use warm-start with z_0 = ER_FB(E_tau[B]).

core_experimental_components.datasets: 21 tasks in 4 domains (Maze, Walker, Cheetah, Quadruped) from DeepMind Control Suite, with unsupervised samples generated using RND (Random Network Distillation) for FB pre-training, and 200 expert trajectories per task for IL.
core_experimental_components.baselines: Offline IL algorithms: vanilla BC, SQIL, TD3-IL, ORIL, OTR, DEMODICE, IQLEARN. Other BFMs: GOAL-TD3, GOAL-GPT, MASKDP, DIAYN.
core_experimental_components.metrics: Cumulative reward achieved by the IL policy, computed using the ground-truth task-specific reward and averaged over 1000 episodes. Policy computation time.

experiment_descriptions.description: Evaluate FB-IL methods (BC_FB, ER_FB, RER_FB, FM_FB, DM_FB, BBELLFB, GOALFB) against standard offline IL algorithms and other BFM methods on 21 tasks across 4 domains, using a single expert demonstration per task. Performance is measured by cumulative reward and policy computation time. Experiments are repeated with 20 random seeds.

analysis_experiments: The influence of the number of expert trajectories on FB-IL and BC methods is studied.
The performance of methods under a shift between initial state distributions at test time and expert trajectory collection is evaluated.
The robustness of the overall approach is confirmed by showing performance is not highly sensitive to variations in the pre-trained FB foundation model across 10 random seeds for FB training.
Ablation studies are performed on the warm-start strategy for optimization-based FB-IL methods.
Qualitative evaluation of imitating behaviors for non-stationary experts is provided.

FB-IL methods will demonstrate superior performance compared to other pre-trained behavior foundation models.
FB-IL methods will be able to implement a wider set of imitation learning principles compared to other behavior foundation models.
Behavioral cloning baselines (vanilla BC) will perform poorly with only one expert trajectory, while BC_FB will show much stronger performance.
Reward-based FB-IL methods will achieve consistent performance across environments and perform on par or better than baselines with the same implicit reward function.
Distribution matching and apprenticeship learning baselines will perform poorly in many domains.
Goal-based reduction methods (like GOAL-TD3) will perform well among other BFM methods but will be more limited in applicability compared to GOALFB.
GOALFB will match or outperform other goal-based methods in imitating non-stationary behaviors like concatenated yoga poses.
FB methods will be less sensitive to the number of expert trajectories compared to BC methods.
Performance will be largely unchanged under a shift in initial state distributions.

paper_name: TabRepo: A Large Scale Repository of Tabular Model Evaluations and its AutoML Applications

basic_idea: Introduced TabRepo, a large-scale repository of tabular model evaluations and predictions.
TabRepo enables efficient analysis of hyperparameter optimization and ensembling by leveraging precomputed predictions.

paper_name: Diffusion Generative Flow Samplers: Improving learning signals through partial trajectory optimization

basic_idea: Propose Diffusion Generative Flow Samplers (DGFS), a framework to train diffusion models for sampling from intractable high-dimensional density functions.
DGFS breaks down the learning process into partial trajectory segments by parameterizing an additional 'flow function', enabling intermediate learning signals.
This approach aims to improve learning signals and credit assignment compared to methods requiring full trajectories.
motivation: Sampling from intractable high-dimensional density functions is a fundamental task in machine learning and statistics.

Existing sampling-based approaches using controlled stochastic processes require full trajectories to compute the training objective, leading to sluggish credit assignment and learning signals only at the terminal time.
Previous diffusion-based sampling methods that train on unnormalized densities struggle with long sequential chains for sampling, causing credit assignment problems.
Popular Kullback-Leibler (KL) problem formulations for these methods only provide learning signals for the terminal state, hindering efficient learning.
Variational inference methods often have limited expressiveness and can suffer from bad learning dynamics.
Monte Carlo methods can get stuck in local modes or suffer from long mixing times.
research_question: Can parameterizing an additional 'flow function' allow for tractable breakdown of the learning process into short partial trajectory segments in diffusion-based sampling?
Can Diffusion Generative Flow Samplers (DGFS) achieve more accurate estimates of the normalization constant than closely-related prior methods by leveraging intermediate learning signals?
Does using partial trajectory segments and intermediate learning signals improve gradient noise and stabilize convergence in diffusion-based sampling?
Can DGFS update its parameters without having full trajectory specification?
Can DGFS receive intermediate learning signals even before a sampling path is finished?

The flow function $F_n(\x_n;\vtheta)$ is trained to satisfy the constraint: $F_n(\x_n;\vtheta) \prod_{l=n}^{N-1}P_F(\x_{l+1}|\x_l;\vtheta) = \mu(\x_N)\prod_{l=n}^{N-1}P_B(\x_l|\x_{l+1})$, where $\mu(\cdot)$ is the unnormalized target density, $P_F$ is the forward transition probability, and $P_B$ is the backward transition probability derived from the reference process.
This constraint allows $F_n(\cdot;\vtheta)$ to amortize the integration computation required for $p_n(\x_n)$ into the learning of $\vtheta$.

Intermediate learning signals are incorporated using a forward-looking technique, parameterizing the log state flow as $\log F_n(\x_n;\vtheta)=\log	ilde R_n(\x_n) + 	ext{NN}(\x_n;\vtheta)$, where $\log	ilde R_n(\cdot)=(1-	frac{n}{N})\log p^efe_n(\cdot) + 	frac{n}{N}\log\mu(\cdot)$.

The forward drift $ (\cdot, n)$ is modeled as $ (\cdot, n) / \sigma = 	ext{NN}_1(\cdot, n) + 	ext{NN}_2(n)\cdot
abla\log\mu(\cdot)$, combining learned drift with gradient information from the unnormalized target density.

The partition function $Z$ is estimated using importance sampling with the forward process $\mathcal{Q}$ as the proposal distribution, yielding a lower bound: $\log Z \ge \log rac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \exp(S(	au^{(b)};\vtheta))$, where $S(	au;\vtheta) = \log \mathcal{P}(\x_{0:N}) - \log \Q(\x_{0:N};\vtheta)$.

paper_name: Which Examples to Annotate for In-Context Learning? Towards Effective and Efficient Selection

basic_idea: Propose AdaICL, a model-adaptive, optimization-free algorithm for selecting which examples to annotate for in-context learning (ICL) given a limited annotation budget.

AdaICL combines uncertainty-based sampling (identifying examples the model is uncertain about) with diversity-based sampling (selecting semantically diverse examples) to improve ICL effectiveness and budget efficiency.
The selection strategy is framed as a Maximum Coverage problem, which is approximated using a greedy algorithm, allowing dynamic adaptation based on model feedback.
motivation: In-context learning (ICL) in Large Language Models (LLMs) is efficient as it requires no parameter updates but is sensitive to the quality and selection of provided examples.
Acquiring ground-truth labels for ICL examples is costly, necessitating efficient selection strategies under a limited annotation budget.
Reducing the number of ICL examples can lower inference costs and meet LLM context length limitations.
Existing active learning methods for ICL often rely on fine-tuning, which is not scalable for very large LLMs, or do not effectively combine uncertainty and diversity sampling.
Current diversity-based methods may select redundant examples or fail to identify examples that help the LLM learn new information.
Uncertainty sampling alone has shown inferior performance compared to other approaches in some ICL settings.
There is a need to select examples that maximize LLM performance while minimizing annotation costs and inference complexity.
research_question: How does the proposed AdaICL algorithm compare to state-of-the-art active learning strategies for in-context learning (ICL) in terms of performance?
How efficient is AdaICL in terms of labeling costs and inference costs compared to other methods?
How robust is AdaICL under different experimental setups, including varying numbers of ICL examples, similarity spaces, and LLMs?

method: The AdaICL algorithm identifies 'hard examples' by querying a Large Language Model (LLM) for its output probabilities on unlabeled data; examples with lower predicted probabilities for the chosen label are considered harder.

Semantic regions of hard examples are constructed using a graph-based approach, specifically an egocentric network (egonet) around each hard example, considering incoming edges from other hard examples within a similarity space (e.g., derived from SBERT embeddings).

The selection of informative examples is formulated as a Maximum Coverage Problem (MCP), where the goal is to select a subset of example sets (regions) that maximizes the coverage of the hardest examples within the annotation budget.
The MCP is approximately solved using a greedy algorithm that iteratively selects the set covering the most currently uncovered hard examples.

AdaICL operates iteratively: it selects a batch of examples, these are annotated, then the LLM's feedback is re-evaluated to identify new hard examples, and the process repeats until the budget is exhausted.

AdaICL variants include AdaICLb (using k-means clustering for regions) and AdaICLp (dynamically re-weighting examples in MCP to prioritize denser regions with exponentially decaying weights across iterations).
The similarity space for constructing regions is derived from embeddings generated by off-the-shelf sentence encoders such as SBERT, RoBERTa, or BERT.
For classification tasks, model uncertainty is quantified by the probability score of the predicted label; for generation tasks, it's the average log-probability of generated tokens.

Default settings: k=5 shot ICL, budget B=20 annotations, SBERT for similarity space, 2-hop egonets with m=5 for AdaICL, 1-hop egonets with m=15 for AdaICLp, T=2 iterations for AdaICLp, theta=0.5 for hard example threshold.

Evaluate AdaICL's performance on different LLMs of similar sizes (6-7B parameters: GPT-J, Mosaic, Falcon, LLaMa) to understand model-specific effectiveness.
Compare AdaICL variants (AdaICL-hard vs. AdaICL-easy) using Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and reliability plots to assess their impact on LLM prediction calibration.
analysis_experiments: Ablation study comparing AdaICL with its base version AdaICLb to demonstrate the advantage of the Maximum Coverage formulation over k-means clustering.

Calibration analysis to quantify how well AdaICL-selected examples align model confidence with actual performance, comparing AdaICL-hard (uncertainty) with AdaICL-easy (selecting examples the model is confident about).

AdaICL is expected to outperform existing methods while using fewer ICL examples during inference, leading to reduced inference costs.

Using AdaICL is expected to lead to better understanding of the task by the LLM, as evidenced by improved calibration.

paper_name: Dictionary Contrastive Learning for Efficient Local Supervision without Auxiliary Networks

basic_idea: Dictionary Contrastive Learning (DCL) is proposed as a local supervision method for deep learning that avoids auxiliary networks and backpropagation.
DCL optimizes the similarity between local features and label embedding vectors to improve performance in Forward Learning (FL) scenarios.
Static label embeddings in DCL outperform existing FL methods, while adaptive label embeddings achieve performance comparable to Backpropagation (BP) and Local Learning (LL) with better efficiency.
motivation: Backpropagation (BP) in deep learning is computationally inefficient due to forward and backward locking, and biologically implausible due to weight symmetry requirements.
Local supervision methods like Local Learning (LL) use module-wise backpropagation with auxiliary networks, which increases memory and parameter demands.
Forward Learning (FL) avoids backpropagation and auxiliary networks for improved computational efficiency, but its performance is subpar compared to BP and LL.
Existing contrastive learning frameworks for FL are susceptible to task-irrelevant information when auxiliary networks are absent, leading to reduced performance.
Auxiliary networks in LL help mitigate the impact of task-irrelevant information, a role that needs to be addressed in FL without auxiliary networks.
research_question: Can a contrastive learning objective effectively perform local supervision without auxiliary networks in a Forward Learning (FL) setting?
How can the alignment between local features and label embeddings improve performance in FL scenarios compared to existing contrastive learning methods?
What is the impact of static versus adaptive label embeddings on the performance and efficiency of local contrastive learning in FL?
Does Dictionary Contrastive Learning (DCL) effectively reduce task-irrelevant information compared to other FL contrastive methods?
Can DCL with adaptive label embeddings achieve performance comparable to Backpropagation (BP) and Local Learning (LL) while offering superior parameter and memory efficiency?
method: Dictionary Contrastive Learning (DCL) is proposed as a local supervision objective.
DCL optimizes the similarity between local features ($h$) and label embedding vectors ($t$) to address task-irrelevant information in Forward Learning (FL).
Label embedding vectors are generated using a one-to-one mapping function ($f_m$) from target labels to $C_D$-dimensional vectors, initialized as standard normal random vectors.
A label embedding dictionary ($D^Z$) stores these label embeddings for $Z$ classes.
Local features ($h_l$) from layer $l$ are represented as $h_l \in \mathbb{R}^{C_h^l 	imes K_l}$, where $C_h^l$ is the feature dimension and $K_l$ is the number of feature vectors.
The dimension of label embedding vectors ($C_D$) is set to the maximum feature dimension across all layers ($\operatorname{max}C_h^l$).
To prevent backpropagation across layers, the stop gradient operator ($sg[\cdot]$) is applied to the input of each layer: $h_l = f_l(sg[h_{l-1}])$.
The final prediction layer ($f_L$) is updated using a standard cross-entropy loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cross}}$).
All other layers ($f_l$ for $l=1,...,L-1$) use the dictionary contrastive loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dict}}$) for weight updates.

The dictionary contrastive loss is defined as $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dict}}=- rac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left[\log rac{\exp(\langle ar{h}_{n},t_{+}^{'}angle)}{\sum_{z=1}^{Z}\exp(\langle ar{h}_{n},t_{z}^{'}angle)}ight]$, where $ ar{h}_{n}$ is the averaged local feature and $t'$ are layer-wise pooled label embeddings.
One-dimensional average pooling ($pool_l$) is used to align the dimension of label embeddings with the dimension of local features for each layer.
Two versions of DCL are evaluated: DCL-S (static label embeddings) and DCL-A (adaptive label embeddings).
In DCL-S, label embedding weights are kept constant throughout training ($\pmb{t}_{z}^{\mathrm{static}}=sg[\pmb{t}_{z}]$) to maintain full forward/backward unlocking for FL.
In DCL-A, label embedding vectors are adaptive, updating their weights at each layer via error signals from $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dict}}$ (this is noted as partially forward/backward locked).

Predictions can be made at any layer by selecting the label with the highest similarity to the layer's feature vector: $\hat{y}=\operatorname*{arg\operatorname*{max}}_{z}\langle ar{h},t_{z}^{\prime}angle$.
A weighted sum of layer-wise predictions can be used for global prediction.

paper_name: Skills-in-Context Prompting:  Unlocking Compositionality in Large Language Models

basic_idea: Propose 'Skills-in-Context' (SKiC) prompting, a method to improve compositional generalization in Large Language Models (LLMs).
SKiC demonstrates foundational skills and their compositional examples within the same prompt context.
SKiC enables LLMs to explicitly ground reasoning steps on foundational skills.
SKiC helps LLMs utilize both provided and internally learned skills to solve complex problems.
Fine-tuning LLMs with SKiC-style data can improve zero-shot weak-to-strong generalization.
motivation: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with compositional generalization, the ability to solve complex problems by combining foundational skills.
Compositional generalization is a critical reasoning ability akin to human intelligence.
Existing LLMs fail to systematically generalize to problems that are significantly harder than those seen during training or in prompting examples.

Decomposition-based prompting methods (e.g., Least-to-Most, Decomposed Prompting) are limited to problems that can be decomposed into a linear sequence of sub-problems and are less applicable to problems with complex computation graphs.
There is a need to unlock the latent potential of LLMs to actively utilize pre-existing internal skills acquired during pre-training for complex reasoning.
research_question: How can prompt structures elicit stronger compositional generalization capabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs)?
Is it crucial to demonstrate both foundational skills and compositional examples grounded in these skills within the same prompt context to improve LLM compositional abilities?
Can LLMs generalize beyond the explicitly provided foundational skills by leveraging their internal pre-trained knowledge when prompted with SKiC?
Does fine-tuning LLMs with SKiC-style data improve zero-shot weak-to-strong generalization capabilities on complex reasoning tasks?
method: Construct a Skills-in-Context (SKiC) prompt, comprising three blocks: (i) a list of foundational skills with instructions, (ii) a few exemplars demonstrating the composition of these skills grounded in explicit reasoning steps, and (iii) the problem to be solved.
Demonstrate explicit grounding of each reasoning step onto foundational skills within the compositional exemplars.
The foundational skills can be manually curated or automatically discovered by LLMs.
SKiC is a one-stage prompting strategy.
Fine-tune LLMs using instruction tuning data generated with SKiC-style reasoning steps.
The SKiC method is designed to be plug-and-play, replacing standard or Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting.
The method involves providing a short, non-exhaustive list of skills and a few (typically 2-10) compositional exemplars.

datasets: Last letter concatenation (with varying word counts, e.g., 4, 5, 12 words)
Addition and multiplication (numbers of varying digit counts)
Dynamic programming (e.g., finding highest sum of non-adjacent subsequence)
metrics: Internal Skill Activation Rate (percentage of skills used in reasoning steps that originate from pre-trained knowledge)
hardware: Specific hardware not detailed, but implies standard GPU clusters for LLM training and inference.

main_experiments: Evaluate SKiC against baselines (zero/few-shot, CoT, LtM, Decomp, etc.) on tasks requiring systematic generalization (last letter concatenation, addition, multiplication, CommaQA-E, dynamic programming) using models like text-davinci-003, ChatGPT, and GPT-4.

Evaluate SKiC against baselines (CoT, ComplexCoT, etc.) on complex reasoning tasks (GSM8K, MATH) using models like ChatGPT and GPT-4, comparing performance on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution (harder) test sets.
Fine-tune Llama2 models with SKiC-style data generated for GSM8K and evaluate on the MATH dataset, comparing with models fine-tuned on CoT-style data.
analysis_experiments: Analyze the robustness of SKiC to different sets and orders of few-shot exemplars on tasks like last letter concatenation and GSM8K.
Conduct ablation studies on SKiC components (skills, skill grounding) on the Dynamic Programming task to assess their individual importance.
Compare the effectiveness of skills discovered by humans versus skills discovered by LLMs (ChatGPT) for SKiC on RTE and last letter tasks.
Compare the performance of SKiC using skills generated by a stronger model (GPT-4) versus the same generative model (ChatGPT) on the MATH task.
Evaluate the cross-task transferability of SKiC prompts designed for GSM8K when applied to unseen tasks like MATH and FOLIO, comparing with CoT.
Perform error analysis on multiplication, QA, GSM8K, and MATH tasks using SKiC to categorize error types (seen basic skills, unseen basic skills, incorrect composition, incorrect copying, others).
Analyze the internal skill activation rate to measure the extent to which LLMs utilize pre-trained knowledge when using SKiC.

expected_results: SKiC will achieve near-perfect systematic generalization across a broad range of tasks, outperforming existing prompting methods like CoT, LtM, and Decomp, especially on harder out-of-distribution examples.
SKiC will demonstrate significantly enhanced complex reasoning capabilities compared to baselines on tasks like GSM8K and MATH.
SKiC will enable LLMs to generalize beyond the explicitly provided in-context skills and actively utilize their internal pre-trained knowledge.
Fine-tuning with SKiC-style data will lead to improved weak-to-strong generalization, enabling models to solve much harder problems with standard prompting after fine-tuning.
SKiC will be robust to different choices and orders of few-shot exemplars.
Both the inclusion of foundational skills and explicit grounding of reasoning steps will be shown to be essential components for SKiC's effectiveness.
Skills automatically discovered by LLMs will be effective in SKiC prompts, making the method more broadly applicable.

Using skills generated by a stronger LLM for prompting a weaker LLM may not necessarily lead to better performance compared to using skills generated by the weaker LLM itself, suggesting alignment benefits.
SKiC prompts will exhibit better cross-task transferability compared to CoT prompts.
Error analysis will reveal key areas for future improvement, such as handling unseen basic skills and improving composition for complex reasoning.

paper_name: ViP: A Differentially Private Foundation Model for Computer Vision

basic_idea: Propose a recipe for training differentially private foundation vision models using masked autoencoders (MAE) and synthetic data pre-training.
Train a Vision Transformer with Differential Privacy (ViP) model using DP-SGD on the LAION400M dataset with a privacy budget of epsilon=8.
Demonstrate that ViP achieves competitive performance on downstream vision tasks compared to non-private models.
motivation: Foundation models trained on internet-scale data pose privacy and legal risks due to the inclusion of personal or copyrighted information.
Existing differentially private (DP) representation learning methods struggle to achieve high utility, often underperforming models with handcrafted features.

Most vision self-supervised learning (SSL) algorithms, particularly contrastive learning methods, are difficult to adapt to DP-SGD due to their reliance on batch-level statistics and entangled sample objectives.
SSL training often requires many epochs, which significantly degrades DP guarantees (increases epsilon).
There is a need for DP foundation models that adhere to privacy and copyright laws.
DP-SGD can mitigate privacy and copyright risks by limiting the influence of individual data points.
research_question: Can a masked autoencoder (MAE) be effectively trained with differential privacy (DP-SGD) for foundation vision models?
Can synthetic data pre-training accelerate the DP training of foundation vision models and reduce the required training epochs?
How does the proposed DP-MAE training recipe with synthetic pre-training (ViP) compare to existing DP-trained and non-private foundation vision models on downstream tasks?
What are the scaling properties (model size, dataset size, batch size) of the proposed DP-MAE training recipe?
method: Utilize Masked Autoencoder (MAE) as the self-supervised learning (SSL) algorithm, chosen for its instance-separable loss function and lack of batch normalization, which facilitates per-sample gradient computation required by DP-SGD.
Apply DP-SGD to train the MAE model, incorporating per-sample gradient clipping with a clipping parameter $C$ and adding Gaussian noise $\mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 C^2  m{I})$ to the gradients.
Pre-train the MAE model on a synthetic dataset generated using the Shaders21k tool to obtain an initial set of weights.
Use the synthetic pre-trained MAE model as initialization for differentially private training on a large-scale natural image dataset (LAION400M/LAION233M) using DP-SGD.
The privacy guarantee is formalized as $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP, with $\epsilon=8$ and $\delta=1/2n$ (where $n$ is the number of training samples) for the DP training phase on natural images.
Employ AdamW optimizer for both synthetic pre-training and DP training.
Use Vision Transformers (ViT) with MAE-base architecture (12 encoder blocks, 768 width; 4 decoder blocks, 512 width) for the encoder and decoder.
Evaluate the learned representations using non-private linear probing and few-shot fine-tuning on downstream classification tasks.
For DP training, set clipping parameter $C=0.1$, sampling ratio $q=81920/n$, and noise parameter $\sigma=0.5$ for the default $(\epsilon=8, \delta=1/2n)$ setting.

datasets: Synthetic dataset: 1.05 million samples generated using the Shader21k tool.
Private pre-training dataset: LAION400M (specifically, a version with ~233 million real images, denoted LAION233M).
Downstream classification datasets for evaluation: ImageNet-1K, Places-365, Places-205, iNaturalist-2021, iNaturalist-2018, CIFAR-100, Caltech101, Aircraft.
Input images resized and center-cropped to 224x224 resolution for downstream evaluation.
baselines: DP-trained models: DP-NFNet, TAN (supervised training on ImageNet-1K).
Non-private models: AlexNet (supervised training on ImageNet-1K), SimCLR (SSL on ImageNet-1K).
Synthetically pre-trained MAE model: (Syn)-ViP (MAE trained on Shader21k).
metrics: Linear probing accuracy on ImageNet-1K, Places-365, Places-205, iNaturalist-2021.
Few-shot fine-tuning accuracy on Aircraft (10, 20, 30-shot), Caltech101 (5, 10, 30-shot), CIFAR-100 (5, 10, 30-shot).
Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K for DP fine-tuning.
MAE training loss (for ablation and scaling studies).
hardware: Not explicitly specified, but implied to be significant for training large models on internet-scale data.

main_experiments: Evaluate ViP and baseline models using non-private linear probing on ImageNet-1K, Places-365/205, and iNat-2021.
Evaluate ViP and baseline models using non-private few-shot fine-tuning on Aircraft, Caltech101, and CIFAR-100.
Evaluate ViP using DP fine-tuning on ImageNet-1K and compare with other DP fine-tuning methods.
Compare ViP against DP-NFNet, TAN, AlexNet, SimCLR, and (Syn)-ViP on linear probing and few-shot fine-tuning tasks.
analysis_experiments: Investigate the effect of scaling model size (MAE-Nano, Tiny, Small, Base, Large) on MAE training loss and downstream performance (linear probing and fine-tuning).
Analyze the impact of scaling the training dataset size (2M, 23M, 233M samples) on ViP's downstream performance, adjusting noise multiplier $\sigma$ to maintain $(\epsilon, \delta_n)$-DP.
Study the effect of scaling up batch size (8192, 32768, 98304) on MAE training loss and ViP's downstream performance, keeping computational budget constant and adjusting noise $\sigma$ for DP.
Examine the training loss curves for different model sizes, dataset sizes, and batch sizes under DP-SGD.
Compare the performance difference between ViP with synthetic pre-training versus random initialization across different model sizes.
Analyze the contribution of synthetic pre-training by comparing (Syn)-ViP with ViP.

expected_results: ViP will achieve higher transfer learning performance on downstream tasks compared to existing state-of-the-art DP-trained models like TAN and DP-NFNet.
ViP's linear probing accuracy on ImageNet-1K will be comparable to end-to-end trained AlexNet.
ViP's performance on downstream tasks will be competitive with, or even exceed, non-private models like SimCLR, especially when considering the larger pre-training dataset size.
Scaling up model size will lead to improved performance for ViP, demonstrating the effectiveness of the training recipe even with larger models under DP constraints.
Increasing the training dataset size will consistently improve ViP's utility, highlighting the benefit of leveraging large-scale data for DP training.
Larger batch sizes will result in better training stability and improved downstream performance for ViP.
Synthetic pre-training will significantly accelerate ViP's convergence during DP training compared to random initialization.
The DP-trained ViP model will demonstrate strong transferability across various downstream vision tasks.

paper_name: ZEST: ZEROSHOT SPARSE FINE-TUNING

basic_idea: ZEST is a zero-shot sparse fine-tuning method that identifies important layers in a neural network for fine-tuning without requiring extensive computation or dataset-specific analysis.
ZEST trains a universal predictor using various zero-shot metrics (static, forward, backward) to rank layers by importance, enabling efficient fine-tuning of only a small subset of parameters.
By fine-tuning only the layers identified by ZEST, performance comparable to or exceeding full fine-tuning can be achieved with significantly reduced computational cost and memory footprint.
motivation: Fine-tuning only a subset of model layers can match or outperform full fine-tuning, reducing overfitting and accelerating the process.
Existing methods for identifying important layers for fine-tuning are not scalable, especially for large models, as they often require training each layer to convergence.
Previous approaches to sparse fine-tuning either suffer from performance degradation or require expensive computational resources.
The optimal subset of layers for fine-tuning is not easily identified and can vary across different models and datasets.
research_question: Can a zero-shot predictor be trained to accurately identify important layers for fine-tuning across different models and datasets?
How do various zero-shot metrics (static, forward, backward) correlate with the actual contribution of a layer to fine-tuning performance?
Can fine-tuning only the layers identified by ZEST achieve performance comparable to or better than full fine-tuning?
What is the efficiency improvement (speedup, memory reduction) achieved by fine-tuning only the layers selected by ZEST compared to full fine-tuning?
method: ZEST utilizes zero-shot metrics derived from a single forward and backward pass to estimate layer importance.

The method collects zero-shot static metrics (mean and variance of weights), zero-shot forward metrics (activations' mean, variance, absolute mean, absolute variance), and zero-shot backward metrics (gradients' mean, variance, absolute mean, absolute variance, plain: weight-gradient dot product).

Additional zero-shot metrics include snip (sensitivity to loss w.r.t. weights), grasp (sensitivity to |grad| w.r.t. inputs), synflow (synaptic saliency based on parameter product), and fisher (norm of activation multiplied by gradient).
A 'contribution score' is established as ground truth by freezing all parameters except one layer (or block) and fine-tuning until convergence, measuring the final performance.
A universal ZEST predictor is trained using the collected zero-shot metrics as input features and the contribution scores as the target labels.
During ZEST predictor training, pairs of examples come from the same model-dataset combination, but batches can contain samples from various combinations to promote generalization.
For inference on a new model-dataset pair, ZEST performs a single forward and backward pass on a single mini-batch to obtain zero-shot metrics for each layer.
The ZEST predictor then assigns a ZEST score to each layer based on its zero-shot metrics.
The top 'n' layers with the highest ZEST scores are selected for sparse fine-tuning.
ZEST is designed to be orthogonal to existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like LoRA and can be combined with them.

datasets: Vision: Aircraft, Cars, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, CUB, Flowers, Food, Pets
Language: GLUE dataset (BERT), Arc-C, Arc-E, Hellaswag, OpenbookQA, PIQA, Sciq (LLaMA)

main_experiments.description: Evaluate ZEST's end-to-end performance by fine-tuning only the layers selected by ZEST on vision models (MobilenetV2, EfficientNet, ResNet-50) and language models (BERT, LLaMA). Compare validation curves and final performance against Full Fine-Tuning and random baselines across various datasets. Also, evaluate the combination of ZEST with LoRA.
main_experiments.datasets: All vision and language datasets mentioned in Step 1.
baselines: ZEST selected layers (e.g., ZEST@3, ZEST@5, ZEST@10)
main_experiments.implementation_details: Vision models trained for 30 epochs with specific learning rates and decay. Language models trained for 3 epochs with specific learning rates and weight decay. Batch sizes and sequence lengths specified for efficiency comparisons.

analysis_experiments: Analyze the robustness of individual zero-shot metrics by computing Kendall Tau correlation between each metric's ranking and the ground truth contribution score ranking for MobilenetV2, EfficientNet, and ResNet-50 on CIFAR100 and CUB datasets.
Compare the Kendall Tau correlation of ZEST's predictions against the best single zero-shot metric for each dataset-model combination.
Evaluate the end-to-end efficiency (memory and latency) of ZEST compared to other baselines for both vision and language models.
Examine the performance of ZEST-selected layers against fine-tuning using ground-truth contribution scores for language models.
Investigate the combination of ZEST with LoRA by comparing performance and parameter count.

expected_results: ZEST will significantly outperform single zero-shot metrics in accurately estimating layer importance across different models and datasets.
Fine-tuning only a small subset of layers identified by ZEST (e.g., 5-10 layers for CNNs, 3-5 layers for LLMs) will achieve performance on par with or even outperform full fine-tuning.
ZEST will demonstrate faster convergence compared to random baselines.
The ZEST predictor will show a strong and consistent correlation with ground truth contribution scores across diverse models and datasets, indicating its generalizability.
ZEST will lead to substantial reductions in fine-tuning latency and memory consumption compared to full fine-tuning.
Combining ZEST with PEFT methods like LoRA will allow for fine-tuning performance comparable to standard LoRA, but with a significantly smaller number of learnable parameters.
ZEST-selected layers will match or exceed the performance of fine-tuning using expensive, ground-truth contribution scores.
ZEST will show improvements in final model performance while accelerating the fine-tuning process and reducing memory footprint.
ZEST will effectively identify valuable layers, leading to comparable final model quality with reduced fine-tuning memory and latency.

paper_name: Stability Analysis of Various Symbolic Rule Extraction Methods from Recurrent Neural Network

basic_idea: This research analyzes the stability of two methods for extracting symbolic rules (represented as Deterministic Finite Automata) from Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs): quantization-based methods (k-means, SOM) and equivalence query-based methods (L*).
The study compares the stability and performance of these extraction methods across different RNN architectures (LSTM, GRU, O2RNN, MIRNN) and formal grammars (Tomita, Dyck).
The key finding is that quantization-based rule extraction is more stable and performs better, especially for partially trained RNNs and complex grammars, compared to the L* method.
motivation: Understanding the internal workings of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) is crucial for evaluating their ability to recognize grammatical structures.
Instability in symbolic rule extraction from RNNs often leads to failures in the extraction process, necessitating better stability analysis.
There is a need to empirically study the stability of rule extraction methods to understand how RNNs, trained via backpropagation, adhere to theoretical limitations.

Prior work has not adequately analyzed the empirical stability of rule extraction methods from RNNs, which is important given the stochastic nature of neural networks and potential generalization issues.
Theoretical guarantees for RNNs do not always provide polynomial time convergence or stability guarantees, highlighting the need for empirical validation.
It is important to evaluate if rule extraction methods can function effectively even when RNNs are partially trained and do not achieve perfect accuracy.
research_question: Does there exist a class of stable RNNs that can cluster internal states to approximate minimal DFAs with high probability, such that the Euclidean distance between RNN states and DFA states is within a small bound?

How do different DFA extraction methods (quantization vs. equivalence query) affect optimal state estimation from partially trained RNNs, aiming for extracted states to be closer to the optimal states of stable RNNs?

method.description: Trained four types of RNN models: LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory), GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit) as first-order networks, and O2RNN (Second-Order RNN) and MIRNN (Multiplicative Integration RNN) as second-order networks. O2RNN's state update equation is $h_i^{(t+1)} = \sigma(\sum_{j, k} W_{ijk}x_i^{(t)}h_k^{(t)} + b_i)$, where $W$ is a second-order weight tensor. MIRNN's state update equation is $h^{(t+1)} = \sigma( \alpha Ux^{(t)} \odot Vh^{(t)} +  eta_1 U \odot x^{(t)} +  eta_2V \odot h^{(t)})$, using Hadamard product for multiplicative integration.

A DFA is defined as a 5-tuple ($Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F$), where $Q$ is the set of states, $\Sigma$ is the alphabet, $\delta: Q 	imes \Sigma ightarrow Q$ is the transition function, $q_0$ is the initial state, and $F$ is the set of final (accepting) states. DFAs are used to represent grammatical rules.

Collected hidden states from RNN computations and clustered them into $k$ groups using k-means or Self-Organizing Maps (SOM). These clusters correspond to DFA states. Transition matrices were created by mapping group transitions for each input symbol. Initial and final states were determined by majority voting. The resulting DFA was minimized using the Hopcroft algorithm. For each model, 5 DFAs were extracted with increasing numbers of states, and the best performing one on a validation set was selected.

Employed the L* algorithm, using the RNN model as an oracle to classify strings and provide counter-examples. This method aims to construct the transition function of states by repeatedly querying the oracle. The approach followed is based on prior work that uses RNN models as oracles for L*.
Utilized the concentric ring representation to analyze language complexity by visualizing the distribution of positive and negative strings within a certain length, arranged lexicographically.

Defined stability based on Brouwer's Fixed Point Theorem and the concept of a stable estimator. Stability of states was analyzed by embedding DFA states in $\mathcal{R}^n$ and considering the transition function as a mapping, estimating error using RMS error or standard deviation from the true fixed point (when unknown).

Used 7 Tomita grammars. Created train (10000 samples), validation (2000 samples), and two test sets (test bin_0: 2000 samples, lengths 2-50; test bin_1: 2000 samples, lengths 51-100). Ensured no sample overlap between sets. Minimum string length was 2, maximum was 100.

Generated datasets for Dyck-2, Dyck-3, Dyck-6, and Dyck-8 languages. Created train (20000 samples), validation (4000 samples), and test (4000 samples) sets for each. Strings are composed of balanced parentheses.

Simulated partially trained networks by stopping training on Tomita grammars when validation accuracy reached a threshold greater than 85%, ensuring no network achieved more than 90% accuracy on validation and test sets. This was done to evaluate extraction stability under imperfect accuracy.

Trained RNN models with varying hidden state dimensions, often set as a multiplier ($s \in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]$) of the minimal number of states ($n$) in the ground truth DFA. Trained across 10 initialization seeds for each configuration.

basic_idea: Propose a three-stage framework (Segment, Select, Correct) for weakly-supervised Referring Image Segmentation (RIS) that does not require mask annotations.
Leverage open-vocabulary instance segmentation to generate all candidate masks for the referred object in an image.

Stage 2 (Select): Select the most likely correct mask from the set of candidate masks generated in Stage 1 by computing CLIP text embeddings for the referring expression and using cosine similarity with CLIP image embeddings of visually prompted versions of the image (using reverse blurring).
Stage 3 (Correct - Pre-training): Pre-train a grounded model (e.g., using LAVT architecture) on the zero-shot selected masks from Stage 2 to align vision and language understanding.

Stage 3 (Correct - Bootstrapping and Correction): Train a referring image segmentation model using a constrained greedy matching loss. This loss aims to maximize the IoU between model predictions and the candidate masks from Stage 1, while ensuring that references to the same object receive the same mask and references to different objects receive different masks.

Constrained Greedy Matching Loss: A loss function that uses a differentiable IoU loss and a matching problem formulation (solved approximately via constrained greedy matching) to enforce consistency between predictions and candidate masks, ensuring that all references for the same object get the same mask and that different objects get different masks.
Zero-shot RIS: Achieved by combining Stage 1 (Segment) and Stage 2 (Select) to directly perform referring image segmentation without any training on referring masks.
Weakly-supervised RIS: Achieved by using the full three-stage framework (Segment, Select, Correct), where Stage 3 utilizes pseudo-masks generated in Stages 1 and 2 for training.

Baselines: Zero-shot: GL CLIP (using FreeSOLO and SAM), SAM + Select, G-DINO + SAM.

motivation: Machine learning in materials science is often limited by the difficulty and computational cost of obtaining detailed crystal structural data.
Representing materials solely with compositional descriptors is challenging due to polymorphism, where one composition can have multiple distinct structures with different properties.
Existing compositional models ignore structural aspects, leading to less effective performance compared to structure-based models.

Real-world material synthesis processes involve frequent atomic arrangement changes, necessitating recalculation of crystal structures when using graphical descriptors, which is computationally intensive.
Doping and alloying can chaotically change material structures, limiting the use of graphical representations.
research_question: Can composition-based models be enhanced by incorporating structural details of crystals?
How can polymorphism in crystalline materials be effectively modeled to improve compositional representations?
Can a universally applicable compositional representation encoder be pre-trained by considering crystal structural information and polymorphism as uncertainty?
method: Construct a fully connected compositional graph $\mathcal{G}^a = (\mathcal{E}, \mathcal{R}, \mathbf{A}^a)$ from elemental composition and ratios, using a GNN as a composition encoder $f^a$.

Construct a multi-edge structural graph $\mathcal{G}^b = (\mathcal{V}, \mathbf{A}^b)$ from atomic positions and lattice parameters, using a GNN as a structural graph encoder $f^b$ to obtain a deterministic structural representation $\mathbf{z}^b$.

Model each composition as a parameterized Gaussian distribution $p(\Tilde{\mathbf{z}}^a|\mathbf{X}^a, \mathbf{A}^a) \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{z}_{\mu}^a, \mathbf{z}_{\sigma}^a)$, where $\mathbf{z}_{\mu}^a = f^a_{\mu}(\mathbf{Z}^a)$ is the mean vector and $\mathbf{z}_{\sigma}^a = f^a_{\sigma}(\mathbf{Z}^a)$ represents the diagonal entries of the covariance matrix, using separate attention-based set2set pooling functions for $f^a_{\mu}$ and $f^a_{\sigma}$.

Train the model using a soft contrastive loss $\mathcal{L}_{	ext{con}}$ that minimizes the Euclidean distance between sampled compositional representations $\Tilde{\mathbf{z}}_j^a$ and their associated polymorphic structural representations $\mathbf{z}_p^b$, while maximizing distances to others.
Add a KL divergence loss $\mathcal{L}_{	ext{KL}}$ between the learned composition distributions and a standard normal distribution $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ to prevent variance collapse.
The total loss is $\mathcal{L}_{	ext{total}} = \mathcal{L}_{	ext{con}} +  eta \cdot \mathcal{L}_{	ext{KL}}$.
During inference, use the mean vector $\mathbf{z}_{\mu}^a$ as the compositional representation and the geometric mean of diagonal covariance matrices $\mathbf{z}_{\sigma}^a$ as uncertainty.

paper_name: Instant3D: Fast Text-to-3D with Sparse-view Generation and Large Reconstruction Model

basic_idea: Propose Instant3D, a two-stage, feed-forward method for generating high-quality and diverse 3D assets from text prompts.
Stage 1: Fine-tune a 2D text-to-image diffusion model (SDXL) to generate a sparse set of four structured and consistent views from a text prompt.

motivation: Existing text-to-3D methods either use slow score distillation-based optimization (hours of inference, low diversity, Janus problem) or are feed-forward but produce low-quality results due to limited 3D training data.

Directly training 3D diffusion models on existing 3D datasets is limited by the scarcity and lower diversity of 3D data, resulting in poor visual quality, shape, appearance, and compositional complexity.

Score distillation sampling (SDS) based optimization methods, while yielding better quality and text-3D alignment, are time-consuming (1-10 hours per prompt), prone to over-saturated colors, the Janus problem, and limited diversity.
Traditional 3D reconstruction methods require dense input images with significant overlaps, which is not practical for generative tasks.
Existing sparse-view reconstruction methods often require per-scene optimization or are trained on limited datasets, limiting their generalization to complex, text-conditioned outputs.

steps: Fine-tune a pretrained 2D text-to-image diffusion model (e.g., SDXL) to generate a sparse set of four multi-view images arranged in a 2x2 grid.

During inference, Gaussian blob initialization is used: a 2x2 grid with a white background and a central Gaussian blob is created, noised, and used as the starting point for denoising to ensure clean backgrounds.

steps: A transformer-based large reconstruction model (LRM) is proposed to directly regress a triplane-based NeRF from the four generated multi-view images.

A shared MLP NeRF decoder maps triplane features to per-point density and color.
The model is trained end-to-end using an image reconstruction loss (MSE and LPIPS) on novel views.
Training uses multi-view renderings of the full Objaverse dataset, with random views sampled for data augmentation and random subsets of 4 input and 4 supervision views selected.
The model has over 500 million parameters and can infer geometry and appearance from just four images without per-scene optimization.

paper_name: Contrastive Diffuser: Planning Towards High Return States via Contrastive Learning

basic_idea: Propose Contrastive Diffuser (CDiffuser), a method for offline reinforcement learning that leverages low-return trajectories to improve policy learning when high-return trajectories are scarce.
CDiffuser groups states from offline trajectories into high-return (positive) and low-return (negative) samples.
A contrastive mechanism is employed to guide the agent's trajectory generation towards high-return states and away from low-return states.
motivation: The performance of offline reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms is highly dependent on the proportion of high-return trajectories present in the offline dataset.
Many real-world scenarios and simulation environments contain a large ratio of low-return trajectories, making it difficult for standard offline RL methods to learn efficient policies.
Existing research has not sufficiently explored techniques to effectively utilize low-return trajectories for policy improvement.
States within low-return trajectories can signal areas where an agent is likely to achieve poor outcomes, providing valuable negative information for learning.
There is a lack of mature techniques to explicitly guide agent trajectories towards high-return states and away from low-return states.
research_question: Can contrastive learning be effectively adapted to constrain generated agent trajectories towards high-return states and away from low-return states in offline reinforcement learning?
How does leveraging low-return trajectories as negative samples through contrastive learning impact the performance of diffusion-based trajectory generation for offline RL?

Does the proposed Contrastive Diffuser (CDiffuser) method achieve superior performance compared to existing diffusion-free and diffusion-based offline RL algorithms across a variety of benchmarks, particularly those with a limited proportion of high-return trajectories?
method: CDiffuser is composed of two main modules: a Planning Module and a Contrastive Module.
The Planning Module utilizes a diffusion-based trajectory generation model to predict subsequent trajectories from a given state.
The diffusion model is trained using a denoising objective (Mean Square Error) between ground truth trajectories and predicted trajectories from noisy inputs.
A return predictor is learned to estimate the return of trajectories, trained by minimizing the Mean Square Error between predicted and ground-truth returns.
The Contrastive Module is designed to constrain the states within the generated trajectories.
States from the offline dataset are classified as positive (high-return) or negative (low-return) samples.
Two strategies for sampling positive and negative states are proposed: Sampling according to Return (SR) and Sampling according to Return and Dynamic Consistency (SRD).
The SR strategy uses sigmoid functions based on state returns to determine the probability of a state being positive or negative.
The SRD strategy additionally considers cluster transitions computed via MiniBatch K-Means clustering on state representations.

A modified contrastive loss function is derived from infoNCE, adapted to handle multiple positive samples and to push generated states away from negative samples while pulling them towards positive samples.
This contrastive loss is applied to the states extracted from the denoised trajectory at intermediate diffusion steps.
The overall objective function is a weighted sum of the diffusion trajectory generation loss, the return prediction loss, and the contrastive loss.
The projection function 'f' maps states to a latent space for similarity computation, and cosine similarity is used.
The temperature parameter 'T' is used in the contrastive loss calculation.
The final action for a given state is extracted from the first element of the generated subsequent trajectory by the Planning Module.

paper_name: Context is Environment

basic_idea: Propose In-Context Risk Minimization (ICRM) to address domain generalization by framing it as in-context learning, where context from unlabeled examples arriving sequentially in a test environment helps the model adapt and improve out-of-distribution performance.
Argue that 'context is environment' in domain generalization, and in-context learning from large language models (LLMs) can lead to better domain generalization.

Introduce a novel approach where a next-token predictor is trained to predict a target label given an input and its preceding unlabeled examples from the same environment as context, effectively 'zooming-in' on the test environment's risk minimizer.
motivation: Existing domain generalization algorithms struggle to generalize to novel test environments, often failing to outperform simple empirical risk minimization (ERM) baselines.

Current domain generalization approaches like invariance-based methods discard too much predictive signal, while marginal transfer methods dilute important signal by summarizing past observations into coarse embeddings.

Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit in-context learning, a powerful ability to generalize on-the-fly to contextual circumstances provided via prompting, suggesting a potential solution for domain generalization.
There is a need to move beyond coarse domain indices in domain generalization towards richer, amortizable descriptions of environments, similar to how context is used in LLMs.

Failure of machine learning systems in real-world applications due to poor generalization across different conditions (e.g., weather, traffic) highlights the critical importance of domain generalization research.
Existing domain generalization methods do not effectively capture 'needle-in-the-haystack' signals present in individual past examples within a test environment.
research_question: Can framing domain generalization as in-context learning, where unlabeled examples arriving sequentially act as context, improve out-of-distribution performance?

How does the proposed In-Context Risk Minimization (ICRM) algorithm, which leverages context from preceding unlabeled examples, compare to existing domain generalization methods like ERM, ARM, and TENT across various benchmarks?

method: Initialize a next-token predictor model (e.g., a transformer) to predict a target label `y` given an input `x` and a context `c`.
Train the model on a dataset of triplets `(x_i, y_i, e_i)`, where `e_i` is the environment index.
During training, for a randomly selected environment `e` from the training set `Etr`, construct input sequences `(x^e_1, ..., x^e_t)` and target sequences `(y^e_1, ..., y^e_t)`.

Update the model to minimize the auto-regressive loss `sum(loss(h(x^e_j; c^e_j), y^e_j))` for `j=1...t`, where `c^e_j = (x^e_1, ..., x^e_{j-1})` is the context of preceding unlabeled examples from the same environment `e`, and `c^e_1` is empty.

During testing on a new environment `e'`, predict `y'_j = h(x'_j, c'_j)` for each incoming input `x'_j`, where the context `c'_j = (x'_1, ..., x'_{j-1})` consists of the preceding unlabeled examples from `e'`.

paper_name: Decodable and Sample Invariant Continuous Object Encoder

basic_idea: Propose Hyper-Dimensional Function Encoding (HDFE) to create explicit vector representations for continuous objects from samples.
HDFE is sample distribution and density invariant, meaning it consistently encodes continuous objects regardless of sampling.
HDFE does not require training and maps objects to an organized embedding space, simplifying downstream task training.
HDFE encodings are decodable, allowing neural networks to reconstruct continuous objects from their encodings.
motivation: Continuous objects, like point clouds, present challenges for machine learning due to varying sample distributions and densities between training and testing.
Existing discrete frameworks are not sample invariant, requiring consistent spatial and temporal resolutions.
Mesh-grid-based frameworks do not apply to sparse data like point clouds.
Sparse frameworks do not provide explicit function representations.
Most existing frameworks require extra encoder training, which is undesirable in data-scarce scenarios.
Vector Function Architecture (VFA) has strong assumptions on the functional form of input functions, limiting its applicability.
Neural operators lack explicit function representations and are limited to mappings between function spaces.
PointNet does not produce a decodable representation and is sensitive to input perturbations.
Kernel methods do not produce explicit function representations, limiting their use to function fitting rather than processing or prediction.
research_question: How can a continuous object be encoded into an explicit vector representation that is invariant to sample distribution and density?
How can this vector representation be made decodable, allowing reconstruction of the original continuous object?
Can HDFE provide an interface for neural networks to process continuous objects as inputs and produce them as outputs?
How does HDFE compare to existing methods for function-to-function mapping and point cloud surface normal estimation?
Can HDFE be integrated as a plug-in module to improve existing state-of-the-art architectures?
method: HDFE represents an explicit function as the superposition of its samples in a high-dimensional space: F = sum(w_i * E(x_i, y_i)).
The mapping E(x,y) is factorized into E_X(x) and E_Y(y) using a binding operation: E(x,y) = E_X(x) tensor E_Y(y).
The encoder E_X(x) is designed such that its similarity with E_X(x') is approximately 1 when d_X(x, x') < epsilon_0 and decays quickly otherwise.
The decoder E_Y(y) is designed to enable reconstruction of function values through similarity search.
The binding operation tensor satisfies commutativity, distributivity, similarity preservation, and invertibility with an unbinding operation.
Decoding is performed by finding y that maximizes the similarity: hat{y_0} = argmax_{y in Y} < F oslash E_X(x_0), E_Y(y) >.
Sample distribution invariance is achieved through an iterative refinement process that identifies the center of the smallest ball containing all sample encodings.
Implicit functions are encoded by summing weighted E_X(x) for points satisfying the implicit equation: F_{f=0} = normalize(sum_{x:f(x)=0} w_x * E_X(x)).
For practical implementation, E_X(x) is set to exp(i * alpha * Phi * x / m) and E_Y(y) to exp(i * beta * Psi * y), where Phi and Psi are random matrices and alpha, beta are hyperparameters.
The binding and unbinding operations are element-wise multiplication and division of complex vectors, respectively.
The normalization of the final representation ensures sample size invariance.

paper_name: A Symmetry-Aware Exploration of Bayesian Neural Network Posteriors

basic_idea: This paper investigates the impact of weight-space symmetries (permutation and scaling) on the posterior distribution of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs).
The research proposes a new mathematical formalism to analyze these symmetries' effects on posterior estimation and uncertainty quantification.
It includes empirical evaluations on real-world vision tasks and introduces a new dataset of model checkpoints for community use.
motivation: The posterior distribution of deep neural network (DNN) weights is a complex object crucial for uncertainty quantification and robustness, but its high dimensionality makes it difficult to study.
Understanding DNNs as black boxes requires deeper exploration, similar to studies on loss landscapes, but focusing on weight distributions.
Reliable uncertainty quantification is paramount in high-stakes applications like autonomous driving.
Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) offer a principled approach to uncertainty quantification but face challenges in scalability and approximation precision.
Existing methods for approximating BNN posteriors have trade-offs in accuracy and computational efficiency.

Permutation and scale symmetries among hidden units can lead to an increased number of local minima and a proliferation of modes within the posterior distribution, potentially reducing diversity in sampled models.
There is a need for a better understanding of how weight-space symmetries specifically affect the Bayesian posterior and uncertainty quantification.
research_question: What is the optimal approach for approximating the posterior distribution of deep Bayesian Neural Networks on real-world vision tasks and architectures?
How does the quality of the posterior estimation correlate with the accuracy of uncertainty quantification in BNNs?
What is the impact of modes within the posterior distribution on model performance and uncertainty?
How can weight-space symmetries, specifically permutation and scaling symmetries, be effectively visualized and understood in the context of Bayesian posteriors?
What is the relationship between scaling symmetries and L2 regularization in BNNs?

How do different approximate Bayesian methods (e.g., Dropout, BNNs, SGHMC, SWAG, Laplace, Deep Ensembles) compare in their estimation of the Bayesian posterior across various datasets and architectures?
Does a 'functional collapse' occur in ensembles of independently trained networks, and how does it relate to in-distribution and out-of-distribution disagreement?
How frequently do weight permutations occur during the training of neural networks?
method: Develop a new mathematical formalism to analyze the distinct impacts of permutation and scaling symmetries on the Bayesian posterior and uncertainty estimation in deep neural networks.

Introduce the 'minimum scaled network mass problem' (min-mass problem) to investigate the impact of scaling symmetries, defining it as the minimization of the L2-regularization term of a network's weights under scaling transformations.

Propose a protocol for assessing the quality of posterior estimation using Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) on high-dimensional distributions by embedding them into Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces (RKHS).

Evaluate various approximate Bayesian methods (Dropout, BNN, SGHMC, SWAG, Laplace, Deep Ensembles) on image classification tasks (MNIST, CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet) using metrics including MMD, accuracy, Brier score, Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Area Under Precision-Recall Curve (AUPR), False Positive Rate at 95% recall (FPR95), and mutual information (IDMI, OODMI).
Analyze the diversity of models sampled from the posterior by measuring in-distribution (IDMI) and out-of-distribution (OODMI) mutual information.
Investigate functional collapse by computing pairwise mutual information between independently trained networks on in-distribution and out-of-distribution data.
Measure the frequency of weight permutations during training by analyzing the Kendall's tau correlation coefficient between successive permutations of network weights.
Release a large-scale checkpoint dataset containing thousands of real-world models across various computer vision tasks and architectures.

paper_name: IMProv: Inpainting-based Multimodal Prompting for Computer Vision Tasks

basic_idea: IMProv is a generative model that enables in-context learning for computer vision tasks by using multimodal prompts.
The model adapts to new visual tasks by inpainting masked regions based on textual descriptions and/or visual examples of the task.
It is trained as a masked generative transformer on a dataset of figures from computer vision papers and large-scale image-text data.
motivation: In-context learning (ICL) for computer vision is not as developed as in natural language processing.
Existing computer vision models struggle to effectively process prompts from various vision tasks, including task instructions and input-output examples.
Generative models trained on large image-text datasets have not achieved strong ICL performance in computer vision.
Previous supervised inpainting models for computer vision tasks require manual annotations, limiting their scalability and generalization to unseen tasks.
Vision-only prompting methods for computer vision tasks suffer from ambiguities and are limited in their ability to precisely describe a visual task.
Textual prompts can efficiently describe instructions and reduce ambiguities in visual tasks without requiring numerous high-quality visual examples.
research_question: Can a generative model in-context learn visual tasks from multimodal prompts consisting of textual descriptions and/or visual examples?
How does training a masked generative transformer on figures from computer vision papers and large-scale image-text data impact its in-context learning capabilities for computer vision tasks?
What is the effect of combining textual and visual prompts on the in-context learning performance of a vision model?
Can multimodal prompting improve performance on tasks like Foreground Segmentation, Single Object Detection, and Colorization compared to vision-only approaches?
method: The IMProv model is an encoder-decoder architecture based on Vision Transformers, similar to MAE-VQGAN.
It incorporates cross-attention layers after each self-attention layer to allow image tokens to attend to textual tokens.
The model is trained to inpaint randomly masked image patches given the unmasked patches and associated textual tokens.
Textual prompts are encoded using pre-trained CLIP embeddings.
Ground truth visual tokens for training are obtained by mapping image patches to indices using a pre-trained VQGAN encoder.
The model is trained using a cross-entropy loss between predicted and ground truth visual tokens for masked patches.
During training, input images are split into patches, and a fixed percentage (75%) are randomly masked.
Textual sentences are tokenized and mapped to CLIP embeddings.
At inference time, the model can be prompted using text, visual examples (arranged in a grid), or a combination of both.
A visual prompt consists of input-output examples and a query image arranged in a grid.
A textual prompt is a natural language description of the task, potentially including task name, location details, and object class.
When only a textual prompt is provided, the model performs zero-shot completion.
The model is trained on a combination of the new Semantic Scholar Computer Vision (S2CV) dataset, the Captioned-CVF dataset, and the LAION-400M dataset.
The S2CV dataset is collected from computer vision papers on Semantic Scholar, containing captioned figures.
The Captioned-CVF dataset is created by adding captions to the existing Computer Vision Figures (CVF) dataset.
During training, mini-batches are formed by randomly selecting data from LAION-400M and the S2CV/Captioned-CVF datasets.
The model uses a ViT-L backbone.
Training utilizes AdamW optimizer with a learning rate of 2e-4 and weight decay of 0.05.
Training is performed on 8 A100 GPUs with a batch size of 2048 for 150k iterations.
A learning rate schedule includes 2k linear warm-up steps followed by cosine decay.
A pre-trained frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 model is used as the text encoder.
A pre-trained VQGAN codebook with 1024 vocabulary size and spatial reduction of x16 is used.
Text conditioning is dropped with a probability of 0.1 during training.
For foreground segmentation, the textual prompt includes the task and object class.
For object detection, the textual prompt specifies segmentation of a 'rectangle shape'.
For colorization, the textual prompt specifies 'Colorization results' and the object class.
For other tasks like depth estimation, normal estimation, and edge estimation, LPIPS is used to compare generated images with rendered annotations.
The model is trained on a combination of unstructured data (S2CV, LAION) and optionally structured data (InstructPix2Pix) for analysis.
The model is evaluated on Pascal 5i for foreground segmentation and object detection, ImageNet for colorization, and a dataset by Wang et al. for other tasks.

paper_name: Leveraging augmented-Lagrangian techniques for differentiating over infeasible quadratic programs in machine learning

basic_idea: Propose a unified approach to compute derivatives of both feasible and infeasible convex quadratic programs (QPs) in machine learning.
Leverage augmented Lagrangian techniques to handle infeasible QPs by finding the closest feasible solution in an L2 sense.
Introduce an Extended Conservative Jacobian (ECJ) that generalizes standard Jacobians for differentiating through potentially infeasible QPs.
Provide an open-source C++ software package named QPLayer for implementing these differentiable QP layers.
motivation: Optimization layers in neural networks can model domain-specific knowledge but may encounter infeasible optimization problems during training.
Existing methods for differentiating through QP layers often require strong assumptions like primal feasibility, limiting their modeling power.
Previous approaches that enforce primal feasibility during training may require additional learning variables and restrict the types of QPs that can be modeled.
There is a need for methods that can handle infeasible QPs during training to enable broader modeling capabilities and potentially improve predictive performance.
research_question: How can derivatives of solutions to potentially infeasible convex quadratic programs be computed for use in machine learning training?
Can an augmented Lagrangian approach be used to define a differentiable mapping for both feasible and infeasible quadratic programs?
Does differentiating through infeasible quadratic programs during training enable the training of a wider range of QP layers with improved predictive performance?
Can an Extended Conservative Jacobian provide a unified framework for differentiating feasible and infeasible convex quadratic programs?
How do alternative formulations for computing Jacobians enhance numerical robustness, speed, and accuracy for training QP layers?
method: Formulate a hierarchical problem (QP-H) that is equivalent to the original QP when feasible, and minimizes the L2 norm of slack variables when infeasible.
Define a nonlinear map G based on the KKT conditions of QP-H, which is shown to be path differentiable.

Define an Extended Conservative Jacobian (ECJ) as the least-squares solution to a linear system derived from the Jacobian of G with respect to primal, dual, and slack variables, and the problem parameters.
Derive efficient forward and backward pass algorithms for computing ECJs, utilizing augmented Lagrangian methods for the general case.
Develop simplified forward and backward pass algorithms for computing ECJs by exploiting primal feasibility of the QP.
Implement the proposed approach in an open-source C++ software package called QPLayer, interfacing with modern learning frameworks.
The QP-H formulation uses a Lagrangian augmented with a slack variable 's' to measure the L2 distance to primal infeasibility.
The ECJ is computed by minimizing the L2 norm of the residual of the KKT conditions of G with respect to the parameters theta.
Forward pass computation of ECJs involves solving a QP using an augmented Lagrangian-based algorithm.
Backward pass computation of ECJs uses the chain rule with the ECJs of the primal, dual, and slack variables, and provides a computationally attractive alternative formulation.
For feasible QPs, the ECJ computation simplifies, and under certain conditions, it reduces to the standard Jacobian.
For feasible QPs in the backward pass, the computation can be further simplified by solving a linear system derived from the KKT matrix of active constraints.

paper_name: ReBotNet: Fast Real-time Video Enhancement

basic_idea: Propose ReBotNet, an efficient and fast deep neural network for real-time video enhancement.
ReBotNet uses a dual-branch encoder to learn spatio-temporal and spatial features separately, combined by a common decoder.
Employ a recurrent training approach where the previous frame's prediction aids in enhancing the current frame, improving temporal consistency and efficiency.
motivation: Most existing video restoration networks are too slow and computationally intensive for real-time applications.
Current methods often introduce latency by requiring past and future frames, making them unsuitable for live video streams.
Real-world videos often suffer from multiple, complex degradations, which are not adequately addressed by single-degradation restoration datasets.
The rise of video conferencing necessitates methods that can enhance video quality in low-lighting or poor network conditions to maintain communication effectiveness.
Existing video enhancement datasets do not sufficiently emulate practical scenarios like video calls and live streaming with multiple degradations.
research_question: Can an efficient and fast deep neural network architecture be designed for real-time video enhancement?
How can spatio-temporal and spatial features be effectively learned and combined for improved video enhancement?
What is the impact of a recurrent training strategy on the efficiency and temporal consistency of video enhancement models?

method: ReBotNet employs a dual-branch encoder-decoder architecture.
The first encoder branch learns spatio-temporal features by tokenizing input frames (current input frame and previous predicted frame) as tubelets using ConvNext blocks.
ConvNext blocks consist of a depth-wise convolution (7x7 kernel, stride 1, padding 3), layer normalization, GELU activation, and point-wise convolutions, with downsampling blocks between levels.
The second encoder branch learns spatial features by tokenizing individual frames into patches and processing them with linear layers, aiming to maintain temporal consistency.
Both branches feed into separate bottleneck mixer blocks.
Each bottleneck mixer block processes input tokens (T) using token mixing (MLP_TM) and channel mixing (MLP_CM) operations, with layer normalization and skip connections.
The token mixing MLP operates on normalized input tokens to mix across the token dimension.
The channel mixing MLP operates on tokens flipped along the channel axis to mix dependencies in the channel dimension.
MLP blocks consist of two linear layers activated by GELU.
The output features from both branches are added together.
A common decoder, comprising transposed convolutional layers, upsamples the merged features to predict the enhanced frame.
A recurrent training approach is used where the previous predicted frame (y_{t-1}) is used as an additional input alongside the current input frame (x_t) to predict the current enhanced frame (y_t).
During training, gradients are backpropagated sequentially from the last frame to the first.
For the first frame during training, the ground truth frame is used as the initial prediction.
